subject: humanities
notes: In the early 1800s, French army officer Charles Barbier developed "night writing," a code of raised dots meant to let soldiers read messages without light.
Barbier's code represented sounds rather than letters and used cells of up to twelve dots.
Louis Braille, a blind student in Paris, encountered the code at about age twelve.
He found that a twelve-dot cell was too large to feel with a single fingertip.
By 1824, Braille had devised a system based on cells of only six dots, each cell representing a letter.
A six-dot cell can be read with one touch of the fingertip.
stem: The student wants to explain how Braille's system improved on Barbier's code. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: By 1824, Louis Braille had devised a reading system for blind people based on cells containing only six raised dots.
choices.B: Louis Braille was a blind student in Paris, about twelve years old, when he first encountered Barbier's code of raised dots.
choices.C: Braille cut Barbier's twelve-dot cells to six dots, small enough to read with one fingertip, and had each cell stand for a letter.
choices.D: In the early 1800s, Barbier, a French army officer, created "night writing" so that soldiers could read raised-dot messages without any light.

explanation.why: To explain an improvement, a sentence must show what Braille changed relative to Barbier's code and why the change helped. The notes give the change (twelve dots to six, sounds to letters) and the benefit (a six-dot cell fits under one fingertip).
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes Braille's system but never compares it to Barbier's or says why six dots were better. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives background about Braille but does not describe his system at all.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows how Braille changed Barbier's code and why the change made reading easier.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains the purpose of Barbier's code but says nothing about Braille's system.
